summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with atypical chest pain, initially evaluated by cardiology, but found to have no acute cardiac ischemia. The pain was determined to be non-cardiac, migratory, and associated with anxiety. He was treated for a complicated urinary tract infection caused by ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli and coagulase-negative staph, which led to septicemia. Vancomycin and macrobid were initiated, delivered via a newly placed PICC line. He developed acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with volume overload, likely triggered by fluid resuscitation and isosorbide, and improved with oral furosemide. His leg edema decreased significantly, and he was transitioned to oral lisinopril for blood pressure and heart protection. His celexa was reduced to 20mg daily per safety guidelines. He was discharged to extended care with a 14-day course of IV vancomycin and oral antibiotics, instructions for daily weight monitoring, and plans for follow-up on blood cultures and electrolytes.
